title: The Hymn of the Undercroft
premise: Ada Marchetti, a late-night radio host in the fading town of Hollow Creek, begins receiving calls from listeners who died the previous week—each one humming a fragment of a hymn she's never heard but somehow knows. When her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, appears on her porch unchanged after thirty years, Ada learns that in 1974, six children made a bargain beneath the town's flooded undercroft to survive a fire, and each paid with a memory. The dead callers are the other five, returning their pieces of the hymn so Ada can complete it and return what was taken before the first frost seals the undercroft for another fifty years. In the end, Ada descends into the freezing water, sings the completed hymn, and offers her own most precious memory—Wren himself—to free the others, emerging alive but hollowed, saved by the found family of listeners who now call in simply to help her remember how to live.
about_author: Astrid Montrose is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent a decade answering calls from insomniacs, grief-stricken strangers, and the occasional voice she could never quite explain. She writes horror about small towns and the debts they bury, and lives somewhere with very good cell reception.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. During her nightly show 'The Undercroft Hour,' a caller named Ruth asks about a fire Ada doesn't remember; research reveals Ruth drowned last Tuesday. Ada tells herself it's a prank, but her hands shake through the sign-off. Emotional beat: denial cracking at its edges.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A second dead listener calls, humming four notes of an unfamiliar hymn that makes Ada's teeth ache. Her producer Marcus notices her unraveling and covers for her on air. Emotional beat: isolation beginning to break as someone chooses to believe her.

chapters.title: What the Porch Remembers
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She finds frost patterns on her porch despite warm October air—and Wren, her imaginary friend from childhood, sitting on the steps, unchanged since 1974. He says only: 'You kept your piece.' Emotional beat: terror braided with a homesickness she can't name.

chapters.title: Hollow Creek, 1974
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Ada reading microfilm, intercut with fragmented third-person scenes of six children fleeing a church basement fire. Five names appear in the obituaries—all dead within the last week. Emotional beat: dread assembling itself into pattern.

chapters.title: Marcus Knows the Hymn Too
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. He confesses he grew up in Hollow Creek and has hummed the same melody his whole life without knowing why. His grandmother was the undercroft's caretaker. Emotional beat: two lonely people discovering shared haunting, tentative trust.

chapters.title: The Flooded Floor
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She breaks into the condemned First Methodist church and finds the undercroft entrance behind the organ, half-submerged in black water. Frost creeps up the walls in patterns matching her porch. Something below answers when she hums. Emotional beat: awe curdling into violation.

chapters.title: Ruth Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. On air, Ruth finally speaks plainly: 'We gave memories so we'd walk out. You were the sixth. You never came back down to pay.' The line goes dead mid-sentence. Emotional beat: betrayal—the survival she treasured was theft.

chapters.title: Mother's Locked Room
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, visiting her mother in assisted living. Her mother, lucid for once, begs her not to go under the church: 'Your father sang it wrong. That's why you're alone.' A photograph shows six children, one face scratched out. Emotional beat: inherited guilt, family as wound.

chapters.title: The Fifth Caller
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Danny, age nine, who died in 1974 yet calls the station from a payphone. He tells Ada the bargain's terms: return what was taken by first frost, or the frost takes the town instead. Emotional beat: innocence weaponized, stakes made concrete.

chapters.title: Inventory of Losses
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. With Marcus, she lists what each child lost: a mother's face, a first love, a language, a name. Ada realizes her 'piece' is Wren himself—that imaginary friends aren't imagined here. Emotional beat: grief reframed as evidence.

chapters.title: The Town That Forgot
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Hollow Creek residents begin losing small memories as frost spreads inward from the church—street names, anniversaries, their children's middle names. The town blames a gas leak. Emotional beat: collective denial, horror going public.

chapters.title: Wren Speaks
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Wren finally explains: he is not her imagination but the memory the undercroft couldn't digest—a guardian stitched from the six children's discarded wonder. If she returns him, she frees them and loses him forever. Emotional beat: love measured against duty.

chapters.title: Marcus Descends Alone
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Impatient and terrified, Marcus enters the undercroft at night with a recorder. He finds pews underwater and faces in the frost, and comes back up missing his grandmother's face from every memory. Emotional beat: hubris and its price; the cost is real.

chapters.title: The Hymn Assembled
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Broadcasting live past sign-off, she lets the five dead callers sing their fragments over the air while listeners phone in harmonies. The completed hymn plays across Hollow Creek, and every window frosts at once. Emotional beat: found family achieving something none could alone.

chapters.title: First Frost
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The frost reaches her porch. Wren begins to fade at the edges like breath on glass. The dead callers give her until midnight—the exact hour of the 1974 fire—to come down willingly. Emotional beat: deadline pressure, tenderness under threat.

chapters.title: What Was Taken in 1974
chapters.summary: Full flashback, third person. The six children trapped in the flooding undercroft during the fire above; the thing in the water offering survival for memories; five paying; little Ada refusing, and Wren stepping between her and the debt. Emotional beat: the truth recontextualizing everything—she was protected, not guilty.

chapters.title: The Descent
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She walks into the freezing water with the hymn, guided by voices on a portable radio tuned to her own show. The frost-thing rises to meet her wearing the faces of everyone she's ever forgotten. Emotional beat: courage as an act of love, not bravery.

chapters.title: The Offering
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, submerged and dreamlike. She sings the final verse and gives back Wren—not as payment but as gift, breaking the bargain's logic. The five dead step out of the frost, restored, and the thing in the water unravels into ordinary cold. Emotional beat: sacrifice transmuted into grace.

chapters.title: Surface
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. He pulls Ada from the water at 12:01. She remembers nothing of Wren, nothing of the hymn, but the town's memories flood back and the frost retreats. Five new listeners call in, alive again, singing softly. Emotional beat: exhaustion, relief, the strange lightness of loss.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Weeks later, she resumes the show. Something is missing she cannot name; she keeps a chair by the window for no reason she understands. Her mother dies peacefully, finally remembering her father's face. Emotional beat: mourning without an object, quiet devastation.

chapters.title: Calls From the Living
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The five restored survivors begin calling the show nightly—not with hauntings but with stories, recipes, apologies, jokes. They become her family of record. One night a caller hums four notes, and Ada's chest aches sweetly. Emotional beat: healing as ongoing practice, not event.

chapters.title: The Hymn of the Undercroft
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Ada's POV. On the last night before winter, frost blooms once on her porch—in the shape of a small bird. Ada smiles, hums the melody she doesn't remember learning, and signs off: 'This one's for whoever's listening, wherever you are.' Emotional beat: bittersweet closure; some loves persist beyond memory.
